stem: In a Next.js 16 App Router project, which file creates an endpoint that answers `GET /api/users` with JSON?

options.text: `app/api/users/route.ts` exporting `async function GET()`
options.why: Route Handlers live in a `route.ts` file and export one named function per HTTP method.

options.text: `app/api/users/page.tsx` exporting `async function GET()`
options.why: `page.tsx` renders UI; HTTP method exports in a page file are not request handlers.

options.text: `app/api/users/route.ts` with `export default function handler(req, res)`
options.why: That is the Pages Router API Routes shape; Route Handlers need named method exports.

options.text: `app/api/users/handler.ts` exporting a `GET` function
options.why: Only the `route.js|ts` file name is a routing convention; `handler.ts` is just a module.

explanation: Route Handlers are defined in a `route.js` or `route.ts` file inside the `app` directory. Each supported HTTP method is a named export (`GET`, `POST`, and so on) that receives a Web `Request` and returns a `Response`. A default export in the Pages API style is not used in the App Router.

stem: A project can have both `app/dashboard/page.tsx` and `app/dashboard/route.ts`, so that browsers get the page and `POST /dashboard` goes to the route handler.

options.text: True
options.why: They can't coexist: each `page` or `route` file takes over every HTTP verb for its route.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: a `route.js` cannot sit at the same route segment as a `page.js`; Next.js reports a conflict.

explanation: Each `route.js` or `page.js` takes over all HTTP verbs for its route, so a page and a route handler at the same segment conflict. Put the handler on its own path, such as `app/api/dashboard/route.ts`, or handle the POST with a Server Action.

stem: `app/api/items/route.ts` exports only `GET` and `POST`. A client sends `DELETE /api/items`. What HTTP status code does Next.js return? Type the number.
explanation: If a client calls a method the route file does not export, Next.js answers `405 Method Not Allowed`. Only `HEAD` (via `GET`) and `OPTIONS` are filled in automatically.

stem: A handler receives `GET /api/search?query=hello`. How do you read `query` inside `export function GET(request: NextRequest)`?

options.text: `request.query.query`, as in Pages Router API routes
options.why: `request.query` belongs to the Pages Router `req` object; NextRequest has no such property.

options.text: `request.nextUrl.searchParams.get('query')`
options.why: `nextUrl` is a parsed URL object, and its `searchParams` is a standard URLSearchParams.

options.text: `(await headers()).get('query')` from `next/headers`
options.why: Query parameters are part of the URL, not request headers.

options.text: `await request.json()` and then reading `body.query`
options.why: A GET request carries no body, and the value is in the URL anyway.

explanation: `NextRequest` extends the Web `Request` with `nextUrl`, a parsed URL with Next.js extras. `request.nextUrl.searchParams.get('query')` returns `"hello"`. With a plain `Request`, `new URL(request.url).searchParams` gives the same result.

stem: Match each incoming request body with the Web `Request` method a route handler should use to read it.

options.text: `await request.json()`
`await request.formData()`
`await request.text()`
`await request.arrayBuffer()`

prompts.text: A JSON body from `fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(data) })`
A `<form>` submission or a multipart upload with fields and files
A webhook whose signature must be checked against the exact raw payload
Raw binary bytes, such as a PDF posted with `Content-Type: application/pdf`

explanation: Route Handlers use the standard Web `Request` body methods. `json()` parses JSON, `formData()` parses urlencoded or multipart bodies, `text()` returns the raw string (what webhook signature checks need), and `arrayBuffer()` gives raw bytes. Each body can be read only once.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: In Next.js 16 without Cache Components enabled, what happens to the response of a plain `export async function GET()` in a route handler?

options.text: It is prerendered at build time and cached until the next deploy
options.why: That was the Next.js 13 and 14 default; version 15 changed GET handlers to dynamic.

options.text: It is cached for 60 seconds and then revalidated in the background
options.why: There is no default revalidation period for route handlers.

options.text: It runs on every request; caching is opt-in, e.g. `force-static`
options.why: Since v15, GET handlers are not cached by default.

options.text: It is cached only in the browser through a default `Cache-Control` header
options.why: Next.js adds no such default; caching is decided on the server side.

explanation: Route Handlers are not cached by default. You can opt a `GET` handler into caching with a route config option such as `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`. Other methods are never cached. The default for `GET` changed from static to dynamic in v15.0.0.

stem: Which statements about Route Handlers are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: They are only available inside the `app` directory
options.why: They are the App Router's equivalent of Pages Router API Routes.

options.text: They do not take part in layouts or client-side navigation like pages do
options.why: A route handler is the lowest-level routing primitive: no layout wraps its response.

options.text: Their responses are wrapped in the nearest `layout.tsx`
options.why: Layouts only wrap pages; a route handler returns its Response as-is.

options.text: They must use a default export that switches on `request.method`
options.why: Each HTTP method is a separate named export such as `GET` or `POST`.

options.text: They can share a folder with `page.tsx` if they only export `POST`
options.why: A route file at the same segment as a page conflicts, whatever methods it exports.

explanation: Route Handlers exist only in the `app` directory and replace Pages Router API Routes. They are the lowest-level routing primitive: they don't render inside layouts, don't take part in client navigations, and can't share a segment with `page.js`.

stem: A `POST` handler creates a user and should reply with status `201` and the new user as JSON. Which return statement does that?

options.text: `return res.status(201).json(user)`
options.why: There is no `res` argument in Route Handlers; that is the Express or Pages API style.

options.text: `return { status: 201, body: user }`
options.why: A plain object is not a Response; Next.js throws "No response is returned from route handler".

options.text: `return NextResponse.next({ status: 201, json: user })`
options.why: `NextResponse.next()` is for Proxy to continue routing, not to send a body.

options.text: `return NextResponse.json(user, { status: 201 })`
options.why: `NextResponse.json` (or `Response.json`) builds a JSON response with the given init.

explanation: Route Handlers return a Web `Response`. `NextResponse.json(data, { status: 201 })` and the standard `Response.json(data, { status: 201 })` both serialise the body and set `Content-Type: application/json`. Returning anything that isn't a Response makes Next.js throw at runtime.

options.text: Dynamic segments are no longer passed to route handlers; read them from `request.url`
options.why: They are still passed, in the second `context` argument.

options.text: `params` is now a Promise, so the handler must use `const { id } = await params`
options.why: Since v15, `context.params` is a promise; a codemod is available.

options.text: The folder must be renamed from `[id]` to `[[id]]` for route handlers
options.why: Double brackets mark an optional catch-all segment, not a route-handler requirement.

options.text: Route handlers now get `params` through `useParams()` from `next/navigation`
options.why: `useParams` is a Client Component hook and can't be used in a route handler.

explanation: Since v15.0.0, `context.params` in Route Handlers is a Promise that resolves to the dynamic segment values. Reading `params.id` directly gets a property of the Promise, which is `undefined`. Await it: `const { id } = await params`. You can type the context with `RouteContext<'/api/posts/[id]'>`.

stem: `app/api/items/route.ts` exports `GET` and `POST` but no `OPTIONS`. What does Next.js 16 return for `OPTIONS /api/items`?

options.text: `405 Method Not Allowed`, because `OPTIONS` is not exported
options.why: `OPTIONS` is one of the two methods Next.js implements automatically.

options.text: `200` with permissive `Access-Control-Allow-*` CORS headers
options.why: The automatic handler sets no CORS headers at all.

options.text: `204` with `Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, POST`
options.why: Next.js answers OPTIONS itself and lists the methods the route supports.

options.text: It calls the `GET` handler and returns its body
options.why: Only `HEAD` falls back to `GET`; `OPTIONS` gets its own generated response.

explanation: If `OPTIONS` is not defined, Next.js implements it automatically and sets the `Allow` header from the other methods defined. In Next.js 16 the generated response is a `204` with the methods sorted, including `HEAD` because it is derived from `GET`: `Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, POST`. It sets no CORS headers.

options.text: Route handlers strip the `stripe-signature` header before the handler runs
options.why: Request headers reach the handler unchanged.

options.text: A `bodyParser: false` config export is needed, as with Pages API routes
options.why: Route handlers have no body parser to disable; that config is Pages Router only.

options.text: Webhooks need `export const runtime = 'edge'` to keep the raw bytes
options.why: The runtime doesn't change the body, and the edge runtime is deprecated in Next 16.

options.text: Re-stringifying the parsed JSON changes the signed bytes; use `text()`
options.why: The signature covers the exact raw payload; whitespace and key order change when re-serialised.

explanation: Signature schemes sign the exact bytes that were sent. `JSON.stringify(await req.json())` produces a different string (whitespace, key order, number formatting). Read the raw body with `await req.text()`, verify the signature against that string, and only then `JSON.parse` it. Unlike Pages Router API routes, no `bodyParser` configuration is needed.

options.text: A body can be read once; call `request.clone()` before reading it
options.why: The stream is consumed by `json()`; a clone has its own copy of the body.

options.text: You can't call `text()` after `json()`, but calling `json()` twice works
options.why: Any second read of the same body fails, whichever method you use.

options.text: `console.log` locks the request, so log it after reading `text()`
options.why: Logging has nothing to do with it; the first body read consumed the stream.

options.text: Next.js gives route handlers a pre-parsed body, so `text()` is unavailable
options.why: The handler gets an unread Web Request; its body methods all work, once.

explanation: A Web `Request` body is a stream that can be consumed only once. After `request.json()`, any further read throws "Body is unusable" or "Body has already been read". Read it once and reuse the value, or call `request.clone()` first and read the clone separately.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: Without Cache Components, adding `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` to a `route.ts` that exports both `GET` and `POST` caches the responses of both methods.

options.text: True
options.why: Only `GET` can be cached; other methods in the same file are never cached.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `force-static` caches only `GET`, and `POST` still runs on every request.

explanation: Only `GET` Route Handlers can opt into caching. The docs state that other supported methods are not cached, even when they sit alongside a cached `GET` in the same file.

stem: A Server Component page calls `await fetch('https://myapp.com/api/stats')`, which is a route handler in the same app. Which problems does this cause? (Choose two.)

options.text: If the page is prerendered at build time, the build fails because no server is listening
options.why: During `next build` there is no running server to answer the request.

options.text: At request time it adds an extra HTTP round trip compared with calling the data source directly
options.why: Server-side fetch to your own app goes out over the network and back in.

options.text: Server Components are not allowed to call `fetch` at all
options.why: Server Components can use `fetch`; the issue is fetching from your own handler.

options.text: Route handlers reject requests that come from Server Components with 403
options.why: Route handlers don't know or care who is calling them.

options.text: The response is cached forever, so the stats never update
options.why: Fetch results are not cached by default in current Next.js.

explanation: Fetch data in Server Components directly from its source, not through your own Route Handlers. A server-side `fetch` needs an absolute URL and makes a real HTTP round trip. At build time there is no server, so prerendering fails. At runtime it is slower than calling the database or service function directly.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: Inside a `GET` route handler, which two of these set a `theme=dark` cookie on the response the browser receives? (Choose two.)

options.text: `(await cookies()).set('theme', 'dark')` using `cookies` from `next/headers`
options.why: In route handlers, `cookies()` can set cookies that are added to the response.

options.text: Creating `res = NextResponse.json(data)`, calling `res.cookies.set('theme', 'dark')`, then returning `res`
options.why: NextResponse cookies write `Set-Cookie` headers on that response.

options.text: `request.cookies.set('theme', 'dark')` on the incoming NextRequest
options.why: This changes the request's cookies inside the server, not the response.

options.text: `(await headers()).set('Set-Cookie', 'theme=dark')`
options.why: The `headers()` instance is read-only; set headers on a new Response instead.

options.text: `document.cookie = 'theme=dark'` at the top of the handler
options.why: `document` doesn't exist on the server.

explanation: You can set cookies with `cookies()` from `next/headers` in Route Handlers, or on a `NextResponse` via `response.cookies.set`. A raw `Set-Cookie` header on a new `Response` also works. `request.cookies` operates on the incoming request, and the `headers()` object is read-only.

stem: Put the steps of a safe webhook route handler in order.

options.text: Read the raw body with `await request.text()`
Verify the signature header against that raw string and the shared secret
Parse the verified string with `JSON.parse`
Process the event idempotently, keyed by the event id
Return a `2xx` response quickly so the sender does not retry

explanation: Signatures cover the exact raw bytes, so read `text()` first and verify before trusting or parsing anything. Webhook senders retry on failures and timeouts, so make processing idempotent by event id and reply with a 2xx once the event is handled. Push slow follow-up work to `after()` or a queue.

stem: A `GET` handler in `app/api/layout/route.ts` reads `const { device } = userAgent(request)` (imported from `next/server`) to choose a layout. A request comes from desktop Chrome on a laptop. What is the value of `device.type`? Type it exactly as JavaScript would print it.
explanation: `userAgent(request)` parses the User-Agent header into `browser`, `device`, `engine`, `os`, `cpu` and an `isBot` flag. `device.type` is one of `mobile`, `tablet`, `console`, `smarttv`, `wearable` or `embedded`, and it is `undefined` for desktop browsers. That is why the docs example writes `device.type || 'desktop'`. Code that checks `device.type === 'desktop'` never matches.

stem: `app/sitemap.ts` builds the sitemap from a database query and uses no request APIs or dynamic config. New blog posts never appear in `/sitemap.xml` until the next deploy. Why?

options.text: Search engines cache sitemaps, so the file itself is already up to date
options.why: The served file really is stale; it was generated once.

options.text: `sitemap.ts` is a special Route Handler that is cached by default
options.why: Without a request-time API or dynamic config, it is generated at build and reused.

options.text: Database queries are not allowed in `sitemap.ts`, so it fell back to an empty list
options.why: You can query a database there; the output is simply cached.

options.text: The sitemap must be generated in `app/api/sitemap/route.ts` to be dynamic
options.why: Moving it isn't required; the metadata route can be made dynamic or revalidated.

explanation: `sitemap.js`, `robots.js`, `opengraph-image.js` and the other metadata files are special Route Handlers that are cached by default unless they use a request-time API or a dynamic config option. Add time-based or on-demand revalidation, or make the route dynamic, so new posts appear.

stem: Server Actions are a good way for a Client Component to fetch several pieces of data in parallel, as a replacement for route handlers.

options.text: True
options.why: Server Actions are queued, so using them for data fetching runs requests one after another.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Server Actions are for mutations and are queued; parallel reads belong in Server Components or route handlers.

explanation: The Backend for Frontend guide notes that Server Actions are queued, so using them for data fetching makes requests run sequentially. Fetch in Server Components where you can. When the client must fetch, use a route handler with a library such as SWR or TanStack Query.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: A `POST` route handler saves an order and calls `after(() => logAnalytics())`. Put these events in the order they happen.

options.text: The handler writes the order to the database
The handler calls `after()`, which schedules the analytics callback
The handler returns its `Response`
The response is sent to the client
The `after` callback runs and logs the analytics event

explanation: `after()` only schedules work. The callback runs once the response (or prerender) has finished, so logging and analytics never delay the user. It runs within the route's max duration, and it still runs if the handler threw or called `redirect` or `notFound`.

stem: In Next.js 16 without Cache Components, which of these exports in a `route.ts` file are valid route segment config? (Choose three.)

options.text: `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`
options.why: Route Handlers use the same segment config as pages and layouts.

options.text: `export const revalidate = 60`
options.why: Time-based revalidation works for cached GET handlers too.

options.text: `export const maxDuration = 30`
options.why: It sets the execution limit, which platforms read from the build output.

options.text: `export const config = { api: { bodyParser: false } }`
options.why: That is Pages Router API Routes config; route handlers ignore it.

options.text: `export const methods = ['GET', 'POST']`
options.why: Methods are declared by exporting functions, not by a config array.

options.text: `export const cache = 'force-cache'`
options.why: `cache` is a `fetch` option, not a route segment config export.

explanation: Route Handlers take the same route segment config as pages and layouts: `dynamic`, `dynamicParams`, `revalidate`, `fetchCache`, `runtime` and `maxDuration`. With Cache Components enabled in v16, `dynamic`, `dynamicParams`, `revalidate` and `fetchCache` are removed in favour of `use cache`.

stem: A link checker sends `HEAD /api/track` requests. That route exports only `GET`, which increments a view counter. The counter climbs even though nobody calls GET. Why?

options.text: Next.js turns HEAD into a 405, and the checker then retries with GET
options.why: HEAD is not answered with 405 when a GET handler exists.

options.text: Browsers prefetch every API route they find in the page HTML
options.why: Browsers don't prefetch arbitrary API URLs, and the checker sent HEAD itself.

options.text: Without a `HEAD` export, Next.js runs the `GET` handler for it
options.why: HEAD is implemented automatically from GET, so its side effects run too.

options.text: `HEAD` requests are routed to `OPTIONS`, which calls every exported method
options.why: The automatic OPTIONS handler only returns an `Allow` header.

explanation: Next.js implements `HEAD` automatically by calling the `GET` handler when `HEAD` isn't exported, and only the body is dropped from the reply. Any side effect in `GET` therefore also runs for `HEAD`. Keep `GET` safe and idempotent, move counting to a `POST`, or export a separate `HEAD`.

stem: A SPA on `https://app.example.com` sends `fetch('https://api.example.com/api/notes', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body })`. The Next.js handler on `api.example.com` exports only `POST`, which returns `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com`. The browser still blocks the request. Why?

options.text: The `OPTIONS` preflight gets Next's default reply, with no CORS headers
options.why: A JSON POST triggers a preflight; export `OPTIONS` with the Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers.

options.text: Route handlers can't return CORS headers; only `next.config.js` can set them
options.why: Handlers can set any response headers, including CORS ones.

options.text: The POST handler must also send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
options.why: Credentials aren't involved here; the preflight fails before the POST.

options.text: Cross-origin requests always need `export const runtime = 'edge'`
options.why: The runtime has nothing to do with CORS.

explanation: A cross-origin POST with `Content-Type: application/json` is not a "simple" request, so the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` preflight. Without an exported `OPTIONS`, Next.js returns a `204` with only an `Allow` header, and the preflight fails CORS. Export `OPTIONS` (or set headers in Proxy or `next.config.js`) returning `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Methods` and `-Headers`.

options.text: A `307` redirect to `/login`
options.why: The redirect never escapes the `try` block.

options.text: A `500` response with `{"error":"failed"}`
options.why: `redirect()` works by throwing; the `catch` swallows it and returns the 500.

options.text: A `308` permanent redirect to `/login`
options.why: Plain `redirect()` would be 307, and it is caught here anyway.

options.text: A `200` response with `{}` because `session.user` is undefined
options.why: Execution never reaches the `return` after `redirect()`.

explanation: `redirect()` throws a special framework error that Next.js turns into a redirect response. In Route Handlers and Server Actions it must be called outside the `try` block; otherwise your `catch` intercepts it. Move the check before the `try`, or re-throw framework errors with `unstable_rethrow(err)` at the top of the `catch`.

stem: A route handler calls `notFound()` from `next/navigation` when a record is missing. The app has a styled `app/not-found.tsx`. What does the client receive?

options.text: A `404` with the HTML from `app/not-found.tsx`
options.why: Route handlers don't render UI files such as `not-found.tsx`.

options.text: A `500`, because `notFound()` only works in Server Components
options.why: It works in route handlers and maps to the matching status.

options.text: A `200` with an empty JSON object
options.why: The thrown fallback error is converted to its HTTP status, not 200.

options.text: A `404` response with an empty body
options.why: Next.js maps the error to a bodyless response with that status.

explanation: In Route Handlers, Next.js catches the error that `notFound()` throws and returns `new Response(null, { status: 404 })`. No `not-found.tsx` UI is rendered, because route handlers don't take part in the page tree. Return a JSON 404 yourself if API clients need an error body.

options.text: `{"ua":"Mozilla/5.0 … Chrome/…"}` from each request
options.why: With `force-static` the handler doesn't run per request.

options.text: The build fails, because `headers()` is not allowed with `force-static`
options.why: That is the behaviour of `dynamic = 'error'`, not `force-static`.

options.text: `{"ua":null}`, generated once at build time
options.why: `force-static` makes `headers()` and `cookies()` return empty values.

options.text: The User-Agent of the build machine, cached until the next deploy
options.why: Request APIs return empty values at build, not the builder's headers.

explanation: `force-static` forces prerendering by making `cookies()`, `headers()` and `useSearchParams()` return empty values. The handler runs at build, finds no `user-agent`, and caches `{"ua":null}`. Use the default dynamic behaviour when a handler depends on request data; use `dynamic = 'error'` to fail the build instead of silently getting empty values.

stem: Cache Components is enabled. Which of these `GET` route handlers is prerendered at build time?

options.text: `return Response.json({ q: new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('q') })`
options.why: Reading request properties such as `request.url` stops prerendering.

options.text: `return Response.json({ version: '1.4.2', name: 'quizMonkey' })`
options.why: It touches no uncached or runtime data, so it can be prerendered.

options.text: `return Response.json({ n: Math.random() })`
options.why: Non-deterministic operations stop prerendering.

options.text: `return Response.json({ lang: (await headers()).get('accept-language') })`
options.why: Runtime APIs such as `headers()` stop prerendering.

explanation: With Cache Components, `GET` handlers follow the same model as pages. They are prerendered when they don't access uncached or runtime data. Prerendering stops at network requests, database queries, async file system calls, request object properties (`request.url`, headers, cookies, body), runtime APIs like `headers()`, `cookies()` and `connection()`, and non-deterministic operations.

options.text: Nothing: `use cache` caches the whole Response for the default cache life
options.why: The directive is not supported directly in the handler body.

options.text: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` above the handler instead
options.why: That option is removed when Cache Components is enabled.

options.text: Swap `use cache` for `use server` so it runs on the server and caches
options.why: `use server` marks Server Functions; it doesn't cache anything.

options.text: Move the query into a helper marked `use cache` and call that from `GET`
options.why: Extract `getProducts()` with `use cache` and `cacheLife`, then call it from `GET`.

explanation: The docs state that `use cache` cannot be used directly inside a Route Handler body. Put the data access in a helper, such as `async function getProducts() { 'use cache'; cacheLife('hours'); return db.query(...) }`, and call it from `GET`. The handler is then prerendered with the cached data, which revalidates according to `cacheLife`.

stem: A Next.js 16.3 handler reads a template with `node:fs/promises` and checks a bcrypt hash. A teammate adds `export const runtime = 'edge'` to make it "faster". What is the right advice?

options.text: Remove it: edge is deprecated, and Node.js supports these APIs
options.why: Edge lacks most Node APIs and is deprecated in this version.

options.text: Keep it, since the Edge Runtime gained full Node.js API support in Next.js 16
options.why: It never gained full Node.js APIs, and it is now deprecated.

options.text: Change it to `runtime = 'experimental-edge'`, the supported spelling
options.why: `experimental-edge` was deprecated back in v15.

options.text: Move the logic into `proxy.ts`, which always runs on the edge
options.why: `proxy.ts` runs on Node.js only, and its runtime can't be configured.

explanation: In Next.js 16 the `runtime` segment option defaults to `'nodejs'`, and `'edge'` is deprecated: the docs say to remove the `runtime` export from route files. The Edge Runtime also lacks many Node.js APIs, such as `fs`, and many npm packages. Note too that `proxy.ts` runs on Node.js and its runtime can't be set.

stem: Which statements about `after()` in a route handler are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Its callback runs after the response has finished being sent
options.why: It is designed for work that should not block the response.

options.text: Inside the callback you can still call `cookies()` and `headers()`
options.why: This is allowed in Route Handlers and Server Functions, unlike in Server Components.

options.text: It runs even if the handler throws or calls `redirect()` or `notFound()`
options.why: The docs say it executes even when the response did not complete successfully.

options.text: It keeps the response open until the callback finishes
options.why: The response is sent first; the callback runs afterwards.

options.text: Calling it makes the route dynamic, like `headers()` does
options.why: `after` is not a request-time API and doesn't make a route dynamic.

options.text: It runs without any time limit, outside `maxDuration`
options.why: It runs within the platform's default or configured max duration.

explanation: `after()` schedules a callback that runs after the response or prerender finishes. It is meant for logging and analytics. In Route Handlers the callback may call `cookies()` and `headers()`. It runs even when the handler errors or redirects, and it is limited by the route's `maxDuration`. It does not make the route dynamic.

stem: A route handler streams an AI answer as Server-Sent Events with `new Response(stream, { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream' } })`. Locally it works, but on a serverless host long answers stop mid-stream after about 60 seconds. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Route handlers buffer the whole stream before sending, so it times out
options.why: Returning a ReadableStream streams chunks as they are enqueued.

options.text: The function hit its time limit; raise `maxDuration` within the cap
options.why: Hosts that run handlers as functions end long-running ones at their timeout.

options.text: `text/event-stream` is not supported by route handlers; use WebSockets
options.why: SSE works, and WebSockets fail on such hosts for the same timeout reason.

options.text: Streaming needs `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`
options.why: A static response can't stream live tokens.

explanation: Some hosts deploy Route Handlers as lambda functions, so long-running handlers can be terminated when they time out, and WebSockets won't work. `export const maxDuration = N` lets the platform raise the limit up to its own maximum. For answers that may run longer, use a background job and let the client poll or reconnect.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: Your Next.js app also needs to accept order creation from a native mobile app. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Expose the existing Server Action, since it is already a POST endpoint
options.why: Server Actions use internal, build-specific action IDs meant for your React UI.

options.text: Have the mobile app request the page and submit its form HTML
options.why: Scraping your own UI is brittle and unauthenticated by design.

options.text: Add a route handler with a stable URL, such as `/api/orders`
options.why: Route handlers are public HTTP endpoints any client can call.

options.text: Put the order logic in `proxy.ts` and return JSON from there
options.why: Proxy runs before routing on matched paths; it is not meant to host an API.

explanation: Route Handlers are public HTTP endpoints with a stable URL and contract, which suits third-party, mobile and webhook clients. Server Actions are invoked from your own React UI through framework-generated IDs and are queued. Use them for UI mutations and route handlers for external clients, sharing the same data-layer function.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

options.text: None: `new URL(next, request.url)` always stays on the same origin
options.why: An absolute `next` ignores the base URL entirely.

options.text: Query parameters can't be read in GET handlers, so `next` is always `/`
options.why: `nextUrl.searchParams` works in GET handlers.

options.text: It is a CSRF hole that only `SameSite=Strict` cookies can fix
options.why: The flaw is the redirect target, not cookie handling.

options.text: An open redirect: `?next=https://evil.example` sends users off-site
options.why: Check that `destination.origin === request.nextUrl.origin` before redirecting.

explanation: When `next` is an absolute URL, `new URL(next, base)` ignores the base, so attackers can bounce users from your trusted domain to a phishing site. The Backend for Frontend guide's callback example checks `destination.origin !== request.nextUrl.origin` and rejects the redirect when they differ.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: Match each route-handler situation with the status code Next.js 16 sends.

prompts.text: An `OPTIONS` request to a route that exports only `GET` and `POST`
A `PATCH` request to a route that exports only `GET` and `POST`

explanation: Next.js fills in `OPTIONS` with a `204` and an `Allow` header. `redirect()` becomes a `307` (`permanentRedirect()` a `308`). `notFound()` becomes a bodyless `404`. Methods the file doesn't export, other than `HEAD` and `OPTIONS`, get `405 Method Not Allowed`.

stem: `app/api/notes/route.ts` exports only `GET` and `DELETE`. What is the exact value of the `Allow` header in Next.js 16's automatic `OPTIONS` response? Type it with methods comma-separated.
explanation: The automatic `OPTIONS` handler lists `OPTIONS`, every exported method, and `HEAD` when `GET` exists (because `HEAD` is derived from `GET`). It sorts them alphabetically and joins them with ", ", giving `DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS`.

stem:
What does the browser receive from this handler?

```ts
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'

export async function GET() {
  (await cookies()).set('seen', '1')
  redirect('/welcome')
}
```

options.text: A `307` to `/welcome`, but the cookie is lost because `redirect()` throws
options.why: Next.js carries cookies set through `cookies()` onto the redirect.

options.text: A `307` to `/welcome` that also carries `Set-Cookie: seen=1`
options.why: The redirect response includes cookies set earlier in the request.

options.text: A `500`, because no `Response` is returned from the handler
options.why: The thrown redirect is converted to a response, so nothing else is needed.

options.text: A `302` with the cookie, since GET redirects use 302
options.why: `redirect()` uses 307 here, not 302.

explanation: When a route handler throws a redirect, Next.js builds a `307` response with a `Location` header and appends any cookies set through `cookies()` earlier in the request. A common pattern, setting a cookie and then redirecting, therefore works without building a `NextResponse` by hand.
reference: Next.js source: app-route module; docs: redirect

options.text: It forwards the user's `Cookie` and `Authorization` headers to a third party
options.why: Copying all incoming headers leaks the user's credentials upstream.

options.text: It passes the partner's response headers straight to the browser
options.why: Upstream `Set-Cookie` or internal headers reach clients unfiltered.

options.text: You can't return `upstream.body` because response streams can't be forwarded
options.why: Forwarding a ReadableStream body in a Response is fine.

options.text: `request.headers` is immutable, so `fetch` throws a TypeError
options.why: Passing a Headers object as `fetch` headers works; it is just unsafe.

options.text: GET handlers aren't allowed to call external APIs with `fetch`
options.why: Route handlers can call any API.

explanation: The docs warn against passing incoming request headers straight to outgoing requests or responses. Build an allow-list of the headers the partner needs and add your own server-side credentials. Then copy back only the response headers the client should see, such as `Content-Type`.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: Without Cache Components, a `GET` handler has `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` and `export const revalidate = 60`. The data source changes at t = 10 s. Put these events in order.

options.text: t = 0 s: the response is generated at build and cached
t = 30 s: a request gets the cached response
t = 70 s: a request still gets the stale cached response
t = 70 s: regeneration of a fresh response starts in the background
t = 75 s: a request gets the regenerated response with the new data

explanation: Time-based revalidation is stale-while-revalidate. Within the window, the cached response is served. The first request after it has passed still gets the stale copy and triggers background regeneration. Once that succeeds, later requests get the fresh response. A request never waits for regeneration.

stem: A host deploys each route handler as a serverless function. Which assumptions in a handler become unsafe? (Choose three.)

options.text: That a module-level variable shares state between requests
options.why: Separate instances don't share memory, and instances are recycled.

options.text: That the handler can write files to disk and read them back later
options.why: The environment may not support writing to the file system.

options.text: That a WebSocket connection can stay open from the handler
options.why: The connection closes on timeout or once the response is produced.

options.text: That the handler can return a streamed `ReadableStream` response
options.why: Streaming responses are supported, within the time limit.

options.text: That `request.json()` can read the POST body
options.why: Body parsing works the same on serverless platforms.

options.text: That `process.env` values are available at runtime
options.why: Environment variables are provided to functions as usual.

explanation: The Backend for Frontend guide warns that on hosts that use lambda functions, Route Handlers cannot share data between requests, may not be able to write to the file system, may be killed when long-running, and can't hold WebSockets. Keep shared state in a database or Redis, and files in object storage.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: A route handler rate-limits logins with a module-level `Map` of IP to attempt count, capped at 5 per minute. In production on a serverless host, attackers still get hundreds of attempts per minute. Why?

options.text: `Map` keys are reset whenever the handler returns a non-2xx status
options.why: A Map keeps its entries until the process ends.

options.text: Route handlers run in a fresh V8 isolate for every single request
options.why: Instances are reused for a while; the problem is that there are many.

options.text: NextRequest hides the client IP, so every attacker gets the same key
options.why: The key isn't the issue; the counter isn't shared at all.

options.text: Each function instance has its own `Map`, so counts aren't shared
options.why: Use a shared store such as Redis, or the host's rate limiting.

explanation: Serverless hosts scale handlers out to many short-lived instances that don't share memory, so an in-memory counter only sees the requests that happen to hit that instance. Keep counts in a shared store (Redis, a database) or use the platform's rate limiting, and return `429` when the limit is reached.
reference: Next.js docs: Backend for Frontend guide

stem: A project sets `output: 'export'` to deploy as a static site. Which route handlers produce output with `next build`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `app/feed.json/route.ts`: a `GET` with `dynamic = 'force-static'` returning JSON
options.why: Static export supports GET handlers marked `force-static`.

options.text: `app/robots-extra.txt/route.ts`: a `GET` with `dynamic = 'force-static'` returning text
options.why: Static export can emit HTML, JSON, TXT and other files this way.

options.text: `app/api/contact/route.ts`: a `POST` that sends an email
options.why: Only GET is supported, because there is no server at runtime.

options.text: A `GET` with `dynamic = 'force-static'` that reads `request.headers`
options.why: Handlers that depend on the request are unsupported in static export.

options.text: A `GET` without any `dynamic` export that returns a constant
options.why: With static export you must mark the handler `force-static` explicitly.

explanation: In `export` mode only `GET` Route Handlers are supported, and they must be marked `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`. They run at build time and their output becomes static files such as JSON or TXT. Anything that needs a runtime server, request data or other methods is unsupported.

stem: A developer writes `export async function get(request: Request) { … }` in `app/api/health/route.ts`. What happens?

options.text: Next.js lowercases method names, so `GET /api/health` works normally
options.why: Methods are matched case-sensitively against the uppercase names.

options.text: The build fails with a type error about the export name
options.why: There is no build-time failure; the export is just ignored.

options.text: `GET` gets `405`; in dev, Next.js logs "Detected lowercase method"
options.why: Only uppercase exports are handlers, and the warning appears only in dev.

options.text: It handles every HTTP method, because a lowercase export acts as a catch-all
options.why: There is no catch-all export; unknown exports are ignored.

explanation: Next.js only treats uppercase exports (`GET`, `POST`, …) as handlers. With only `get` exported, no GET handler exists, so `GET` and `HEAD` get `405` and `OPTIONS` returns its automatic 204. In development Next.js logs "Detected lowercase method 'get' … Export the uppercase 'GET' method name". In production the 405 appears with no hint.

stem: A handler is typed with `ctx: RouteContext<'/users/[id]'>`. Locally `next dev` is fine, but a fresh CI job runs `tsc --noEmit` before building and fails with "Cannot find name 'RouteContext'". What is the fix?

options.text: Add `import { RouteContext } from 'next/server'` to the handler
options.why: It is a global helper type, not an export you import.

options.text: Run `next typegen` (or a `next build`) before running `tsc`
options.why: RouteContext is generated during `next dev`, `next build` or `next typegen`.

options.text: Replace it with `{ params: { id: string } }`, which tsc understands
options.why: That compiles but is wrong: params is a Promise in Next 15+.

options.text: Enable `typedRoutes: true` in `next.config.ts`, which declares it globally
options.why: The helper exists only after type generation runs.

explanation: `RouteContext` (like `PageProps` and `LayoutProps`) is a globally available helper that only exists after Next.js generates route types. That happens during `next dev`, `next build` or `next typegen`. A clean CI checkout running `tsc` first has no generated types, so run `next typegen` before type-checking.

stem: Calling `after(() => log())` in a `GET` route handler makes that handler dynamic, in the same way that calling `headers()` does.

options.text: True
options.why: `after` is not a request-time API, so it doesn't change whether a route is static or dynamic.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `after` leaves static handlers static, and in a static route the callback runs at build or revalidation time.

explanation: The `after` docs say it is not a request-time API and does not make a route dynamic. In a static route, the callback runs at build time or whenever the route is revalidated, not for each request, which surprises people who use it for per-request analytics.

stem: Without Cache Components, `app/api/posts/[id]/route.ts` exports `generateStaticParams` returning ids 1, 2 and 3, plus `export const dynamicParams = false`. What does `GET /api/posts/4` return?

options.text: It runs the handler at request time, then caches the result
options.why: That is the `dynamicParams = true` default, not this config.

options.text: A `404`, because only the listed params are served
options.why: `dynamicParams = false` limits the route to the listed paths.

options.text: The cached response for id 3, the nearest match
options.why: Params are matched exactly; there is no nearest-match fallback.

options.text: A `500`, because the handler can't run for unlisted params
options.why: Next.js answers with a 404 before the handler runs.

explanation: `generateStaticParams` works with dynamic Route Handlers to prerender responses for the listed params. With the default `dynamicParams = true`, other params are handled at request time. With `export const dynamicParams = false`, only the listed paths are served and the rest return 404.
